lessons.title: The SOC Mission and Why It Exists

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's own 2 a.m. laptop example as a model, write your own fictional incident (3-4 sentences) that only works if monitoring, detection, and response are all present, then go back through it and remove each of the three verbs one at a time, writing one sentence per verb explaining exactly what would go wrong without it. Then write a one-paragraph justification memo, as if pitching a SOC budget to a skeptical CFO, naming the three real reasons organizations pay for one (regulatory requirements, breach-cost reduction, customer trust) and citing one named framework (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, or SOX) by name.
slots.deliverable: A written fictional incident demonstrating the monitor-detect-respond pipeline, 3 sentences explaining what breaks when each verb is removed, and a one-paragraph SOC budget justification memo naming all three real reasons and citing a specific regulatory framework.

lessons.title: Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 Analyst Roles

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own version of the lesson's failed-logins-then-success scenario, but change the details (different account type, different location pattern) so it's not a copy. Walk it through all three tiers in writing: what Tier 1 can determine and whether they close or escalate it, what additional access/tooling lets Tier 2 make the real call, and what Tier 3 might do afterward (a new rule, a hunt) that neither tier below them could have done on their own.
slots.deliverable: An original failed-login-then-success scenario walked through in writing across all three tiers, naming specifically what each tier checks, decides, and who owns the escalation decision.

lessons.title: Shift Models and 24x7 Coverage

slots.practicalActivity: Design a realistic 24x7 coverage plan for a fictional mid-size company with one physical office and 6 analysts (the exact situation the lesson's Check Yourself question poses). Decide and justify in writing which combination of follow-the-sun, rotating shifts, and on-call escalation actually applies given they only have one office, then sketch the actual shift rotation (who's on nights, how often it rotates) and name who gets paged for a high-severity alert during the smallest-staffed window.
slots.deliverable: A written 24x7 coverage plan for a fictional single-office, 6-analyst SOC naming the specific combination of shift models used, a sketched rotation schedule, and a named on-call escalation path for the thinnest-staffed hours.

lessons.title: SOC Maturity Models: Reactive to Proactive

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's slow-exfiltration example as a template, invent your own scenario where a purely reactive SOC would miss something indefinitely because no rule ever fires on it. Write one sentence explaining why reactive monitoring misses it, then write out, in order, how a SOC would layer proactive practices on top of its reactive baseline to catch it eventually — naming which of the three proactive practices (threat hunting, continuous improvement, metrics-driven management) actually surfaces your scenario and why the other two wouldn't.
slots.deliverable: An original 'never fires' detection-gap scenario, a written explanation of why a reactive SOC misses it, and identification of the one proactive practice (hunting, rule tuning, or metrics) that would actually catch it, with the other two ruled out in writing.

lessons.title: What a SIEM Actually Does

slots.practicalActivity: Take the lesson's port-scan-then-AV-alert scenario and rewrite it with your own two unrelated-looking log events from different sources. Walk your version through all four SIEM functions in writing — what gets centralized, what correlation ties your two events together and how, what the resulting alert says, and how long you'd argue the underlying logs should be retained and why (citing PCI-DSS or HIPAA retention requirements as the lesson does).
slots.deliverable: An original two-event correlation scenario walked through all four SIEM functions (centralize, correlate, alert, retain) in writing, including a retention-period justification citing a named compliance framework.

lessons.title: Log Aggregation, Normalization, and Correlation

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 fake raw log lines for the exact same login event as if logged by 3 different vendors (e.g. a Windows-style EventID line, a Cisco-style syslog line, a generic JSON API line), deliberately naming the source-IP field differently in each (src_ip, SourceAddress, sourceIPAddress). Then build a normalization table mapping all 3 vendor field names to one common field name, and write the correlation logic in plain English that only works once all 3 are normalized to that shared name.
slots.deliverable: 3 original fake log lines for the same event in 3 different vendor formats with differently-named IP fields, a normalization table mapping all 3 to one common field, and a written explanation of the correlation that only becomes possible after normalization.

lessons.title: SIEM vs. Log Management: The Real Difference

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page comparison memo contrasting a fictional company's 'we centralize all our logs in one searchable system' claim (the lesson's own Check Yourself question) against what a real SIEM would add on top. Use the lesson's own port-scan-across-three-systems example as your test case: write out what happens in that exact scenario with log management alone versus with a real SIEM watching the same logs, concluding with a one-sentence verdict on whether the company's claim means they actually have a SIEM.
slots.deliverable: A one-page memo contrasting log management against a real SIEM using the same failed-logins-across-three-systems test case for both, ending in a written verdict on whether 'we centralize our logs' proves a company has a SIEM.

lessons.title: Major SIEM Platforms: A Practical Overview

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 4-row comparison table of Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, and the Elastic Stack, with columns for query language, what each is most known for, and deployment model. Then take the lesson's own example question ('find traffic from IP 203.0.113.9') and translate it between SPL and KQL yourself without looking at the lesson's syntax, writing both queries side by side to prove the underlying logic is identical.
slots.deliverable: A 4-platform comparison table (Splunk/Sentinel/QRadar/Elastic) covering query language and strengths, plus your own side-by-side SPL and KQL query translation for the same question proving the underlying logic matches.

lessons.title: Syslog and the Standard Log Formats

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 original fake syslog lines (not the lesson's firewall example), each with a different PRI value you calculate yourself from a chosen facility and severity (facility x 8 + severity), and decode all 3 back into their severity names using the eight-level table. Then write one CEF-formatted version of one of your 3 lines, with correctly pipe-delimited header fields and key=value pairs for src, dst, and a port.
slots.deliverable: 3 original syslog lines with hand-calculated PRI values decoded back to their severity names, plus one of them rewritten in valid CEF format with pipe-delimited header fields and key=value src/dst/port pairs.

lessons.title: Windows Event Forwarding into a SIEM

slots.practicalActivity: Design a WEF deployment for a fictional company with a headquarters and 3 branch offices, deciding in writing whether each branch uses a source-initiated (GPO-pushed) or collector-initiated (pull) subscription, and why. Then write the subscription's target: which Security log Event ID it should collect (use 4625, failed logons, as the lesson does) and name the exact WinRM port the deployment would use for HTTPS.
slots.deliverable: A written WEF deployment plan for a 4-site company naming source-initiated vs. collector-initiated per site with justification, the target Event ID being collected, and the correct WinRM HTTPS port.

lessons.title: SIEM Agents vs. Agentless Collection

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 10-device log-source inventory table for a fictional environment (mix of domain controllers, workstations, firewalls, a load balancer, a legacy switch, a cloud service) and classify each as agent-based or agentless, writing one sentence of justification per device citing the lesson's actual tradeoffs (overhead, local buffering, completeness, deployment speed).
slots.deliverable: A 10-device log-source inventory table with each device classified agent-based or agentless and a one-sentence, tradeoff-specific justification for each classification.

lessons.title: Log Parsing and Field Extraction

slots.practicalActivity: Take the lesson's own raw syslog line and parse it by hand into the same 6 named fields (severity, process, event_type, dest_user, src_ip, src_port) it shows. Then build your own 3-row normalization table showing the same 'source IP' concept logged under 3 different field names (src_ip, SourceAddress, sourceIPAddress) and write the one correlation rule, in plain English, that would silently break if normalization were skipped.
slots.deliverable: The lesson's raw syslog line hand-parsed into its 6 named fields, a 3-row normalization table for 'source IP' across 3 differently-named vendor fields, and a written example of a correlation rule that breaks without normalization.

lessons.title: What a Correlation Rule Actually Is

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the five-piece shape (event source, condition, time window, threshold/sequence, action) for an original correlation rule idea of your own — not the brute-force example — such as a privileged account used outside business hours. Then write one paragraph explaining what happens to your rule's usefulness if you remove the time window, using the lesson's own reasoning about password typos accumulating over a year versus within 10 minutes.
slots.deliverable: An original correlation rule idea broken into all five required pieces, plus a written paragraph explaining what breaks about it with the time window removed.

lessons.title: Writing a Real-World Correlation Rule

slots.practicalActivity: Using the exact vendor-neutral pseudocode format from the lesson (RULE/SOURCE/GROUP BY/IF/THEN), write a complete new correlation rule for a different scenario: the same user account authenticating to 3 or more distinct systems within 2 minutes. Name the correct grouping key, write the threshold and time window clause, and write one sentence explaining why grouping by user account (not by source IP) is the right choice for your scenario, mirroring the lesson's shared-VPN-gateway caution.
slots.deliverable: A complete original correlation rule written in the lesson's exact RULE/SOURCE/GROUP BY/IF/THEN pseudocode format for a multi-system rapid-authentication pattern, with a written justification for the chosen grouping key.

lessons.title: Rule Tuning and Reducing False Positives

slots.practicalActivity: Invent a fictional noisy rule of your own (not the backup-account example) that's firing too often in its first weeks live, and write a tuning memo proposing both fixes from the lesson: a specific threshold adjustment with your reasoning for the new numbers, and a specific, named exclusion for a known-benign source. Then write one paragraph explaining, in your own words, why alert fatigue from this untuned rule is a security risk and not just an inconvenience.
slots.deliverable: A tuning memo for an original noisy correlation rule proposing a specific threshold change and a specific named exclusion, plus a written paragraph explaining the real security risk of the resulting alert fatigue.

lessons.title: Use-Case Development: Building Detections That Matter

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real risk other than lateral movement (e.g. data exfiltration via personal cloud storage, or credential stuffing against a customer-facing login) and walk the lesson's full use-case development process against it: what it looks like in logs, which log sources actually carry that signal, what the pattern looks like once grouped and timed correctly, and the resulting correlation rule logic (GROUP BY / WITHIN / THEN) in the same shape the lesson used for lateral movement.
slots.deliverable: A complete use-case development writeup for an original risk, answering all 4 of the lesson's framework questions and ending in correlation rule logic in the GROUP BY/WITHIN/THEN shape.

lessons.title: The Real Alert Triage Process

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 original alert scenarios (not the lesson's admin-travel example), one for each of the three triage outcomes — true positive, false positive, and benign true positive — making sure the benign true positive one is genuinely accurate-but-legitimate activity, not an obviously fake alert. For each, write one sentence stating which outcome it is and the specific detail that proves it.
slots.deliverable: 3 original alert scenarios, one for each triage outcome (true positive, false positive, benign true positive), each with a one-sentence classification and the specific proof detail.

lessons.title: Validating, Scoping, and Escalating an Alert

slots.practicalActivity: Write an original alert scenario and walk it through validation (what raw data you'd check and what it shows) and scoping (what else you'd check for spread) exactly as the lesson's file-share example does, ending with a written escalate-or-not decision that explicitly cites which of the 3 escalation criteria (confirmed malicious, unclear scope, needs deeper tools) applies or doesn't.
slots.deliverable: An original alert walked through validation and scoping in writing, ending in an escalate-or-not decision that names the specific escalation criterion applied (or explains why none apply).

lessons.title: Writing a Clear Investigation Case Note

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's own alert (or one of your own), write two case notes for the identical outcome: first a vague one ('looked into it, seems fine'), then a clear one covering all 5 required elements (what happened, what was checked, what was found, what action was taken, timestamps) in the lesson's timestamped format. Write one sentence naming the specific harm the vague version would cause if this same account showed up in a real incident 3 months later.
slots.deliverable: A vague case note and a full 5-element, timestamped case note written for the same alert outcome, plus a written sentence on the specific real-world harm the vague version would cause later.

lessons.title: When and How to Escalate to Tier 2

slots.practicalActivity: Take the alert you escalated in the previous lesson and write a complete, clean escalation handoff containing the 4 required pieces: the classification already reached, the scope already established, the evidence gathered, and a clear reason for escalating citing the specific criterion involved. Decide and justify in writing which real channel it should travel through (ticketing system alone, or ticketing plus a direct handoff) based on the severity you'd assign it.
slots.deliverable: A complete escalation handoff for your earlier alert containing all 4 required pieces, plus a written, severity-justified decision on which escalation channel it should use.

lessons.title: Building a SOC Dashboard That Analysts Actually Use

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch (in writing or as a simple list/wireframe) a cluttered 12-panel SOC dashboard like the lesson's example, labeling which panels are vanity metrics. Then redesign it down to the lesson's 3 real panels (open Sev-1/Sev-2 queue sorted oldest-first, queue depth with a trend arrow, and systems under active investigation), and write one sentence justifying why each vanity panel you cut doesn't change what an analyst does in the next five minutes.
slots.deliverable: A sketched 12-panel cluttered dashboard with vanity metrics labeled, redesigned down to the lesson's 3 action-oriented panels, with a written justification for each cut panel.

lessons.title: Key SOC Metrics: MTTD and MTTR

slots.practicalActivity: Invent your own set of 4 timestamps for a fictional incident (attack start, detection, escalation, resolution) different from the lesson's worked example, and calculate MTTD and MTTR from them by hand, showing the subtraction. Then write one paragraph interpreting what a SOC with your MTTD/MTTR numbers held flat for 3 months, compared to the prior quarter, would tell leadership about where the SOC has and hasn't improved.
slots.deliverable: An original 4-timestamp incident timeline with hand-calculated MTTD and MTTR, plus a written paragraph interpreting what those numbers would mean as a 3-month trend.

lessons.title: Alert Volume and Analyst Workload Metrics

slots.practicalActivity: Invent your own 2-month alert-volume and workload dataset (total alerts per shift, alerts per analyst, average time per alert, backlog carried over) showing the same kind of warning pattern the lesson's example does, then write a one-paragraph analysis identifying which of the lesson's 3 real risks — tuning gap, staffing gap, or alert fatigue/burnout — your numbers point to and why reading any single number alone wouldn't have caught it.
slots.deliverable: An original 2-month alert-volume and workload dataset showing a real warning pattern, with a written analysis naming the specific risk (tuning/staffing/fatigue) it reveals and why no single metric alone would show it.

lessons.title: Reporting Up: Communicating with Leadership

slots.practicalActivity: Take a fictional month of SOC statistics you invent (total events, alerts fired, false positives closed, true positives escalated, an MTTD/MTTR trend) and write the same month two ways: first as the 'accurate but useless' technical report the lesson criticizes, then as a leadership report using the lesson's 3 required elements (plain-language risk statement, trend not a snapshot, a specific ask tied to a number).
slots.deliverable: The same fictional month of SOC data written up twice — once as a raw technical statistics report, once as a leadership report with a risk statement, a trend, and a specific numeric ask.

lessons.title: What SOAR Actually Is and Why It Matters

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a SOC workflow other than the lesson's general description (e.g. a malware alert from an EDR tool that also needs a ticket opened and a host isolated) and write, in your own words, exactly what the orchestration piece connects, what the automation piece runs without a human, and what the response piece actually does — keeping all three clearly separate rather than blurred into one idea.
slots.deliverable: A written breakdown of an original SOC workflow into its distinct orchestration, automation, and response pieces, each described specifically rather than as one blurred concept.

lessons.title: Playbooks: Automating the Repeatable Steps

slots.practicalActivity: Design an original playbook (not the phishing-report example) for a different repeatable, well-understood SOC scenario — such as a malware detection alert from an endpoint, or a blocked-but-repeated login from a known-bad IP. Write it out using the lesson's exact TRIGGER / numbered-steps / IF-branch format, then write one sentence justifying why your scenario meets both required conditions (repeatable and well-understood).
slots.deliverable: An original playbook written in the lesson's TRIGGER/numbered-steps/IF-branch pseudocode format for a new scenario, with a written justification for why it qualifies as repeatable and well-understood.

lessons.title: SOAR and the Analyst Relationship: Not a Replacement

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 original scenarios, one for each of the lesson's 'still needs a human' categories (a novel attack pattern, an ambiguous alert needing business context, and a playbook edge case), different from the lesson's VP-on-a-red-eye example. For each, write one sentence explaining specifically why no playbook could have handled it.
slots.deliverable: 3 original scenarios, one per human-required category from the lesson, each with a written sentence explaining specifically why a playbook couldn't have handled it.

lessons.title: A Worked SOAR Playbook Example

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a trigger other than a forwarded phishing email (e.g. an EDR alert for a suspicious process) and walk a complete playbook through all 5 of the lesson's steps — ingest, extract, enrich, branch and respond, notify either way — writing out both the confirmed-malicious and inconclusive branches in the lesson's IF/THEN format. Write one sentence explaining why the analyst still gets notified even on the fully-automated branch.
slots.deliverable: A complete original SOAR playbook walked through all 5 steps (ingest, extract, enrich, branch/respond, notify) with both branches written in IF/THEN pseudocode, plus a written explanation of why notification still happens on the automated branch.

lessons.title: Lab: Triaging a Queue of Real-Looking Alerts
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Day in the SOC

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own version of this lesson's 3-alert queue — 3 new scenarios involving a login or account anomaly, each starting from the same 'new location' or 'unusual activity' signal but resolving to a different one of the 3 outcomes (false positive, benign true positive, escalate now), the same twist the lesson built with Alerts A, B, and C. Run the full validate-scope-classify process against all 3 in writing, exactly as Jordan does, citing Chapter 5's actual escalation criteria for the one that escalates.
slots.deliverable: An original 3-alert queue mirroring the lesson's structure (same starting signal, 3 different real outcomes), each one fully validated, scoped, and classified in writing, with the escalating alert citing the specific criterion met.

lessons.title: Lab: Writing a Correlation Rule for a Known Pattern
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Day in the SOC

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's exact WHEN / GROUP BY / WITHIN / THEN shape, write a new standing correlation rule for a different known pattern — such as the same account downloading an unusually large volume of data across multiple systems in a short window. Calculate your own threshold logic (not copied from the impossible-travel math), then add one tuning exception for a known-benign source the way the lesson added the corporate VPN exit-node exception.
slots.deliverable: A new standing correlation rule written in the lesson's WHEN/GROUP BY/WITHIN/THEN format for an original known pattern, with its own calculated threshold logic and one written tuning exception.

lessons.title: Case Study: A Full Shift, From Alert to Resolution
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Day in the SOC

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own full-shift case study, different from the Nguyen business-email-compromise example, that walks one incident through every chapter's contribution in order: the raw log source (Ch. 3), the correlation logic that raised it (Ch. 4), Tier 1 triage (Ch. 5), a Tier 2 investigation finding, the resolution steps taken, which parts a SOAR playbook would run automatically (Ch. 7), and what it leaves on the dashboard and in a leadership report (Ch. 6).
slots.deliverable: An original full-shift case study walking one incident through all 7 of the course's chapter contributions in order, ending with its dashboard and leadership-reporting impact.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: SOC Operations & SIEM Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: A Day in the SOC

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own chapter-by-chapter map of this course like the lesson's own recap, but tie each chapter to your own full-shift case study from the previous lesson instead of the Nguyen example, naming specifically what each chapter contributed to catching and resolving your incident. Then write one real resume bullet naming the specific SOC skills and tools you can now claim (SIEM correlation rules, triage workflow, SOAR playbooks, dashboard metrics), and a one-paragraph answer to the lesson's own Check Yourself question about which chapter would have been hardest to remove from your case.
slots.deliverable: A chapter-by-chapter map tying all 8 chapters to your own case study from the previous lesson, a written resume bullet naming specific SOC skills, and a one-paragraph answer on which chapter was most load-bearing in your case.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can function as a real Tier 1 SOC analyst from day one: explain what a SIEM actually does versus plain log management, read and decode a raw syslog or CEF log line, and build or tune a vendor-neutral correlation rule (grouping key, time window, threshold) for a real attack pattern like brute-force logins or impossible travel. They can run the full validate-scope-classify triage loop on a queue of real-looking alerts, correctly tell a true positive from a benign true positive, write a clean 5-element case note, and escalate a confirmed incident to Tier 2 with the classification, scope, evidence, and reason a clean handoff requires. They can also design a 3-panel action-oriented SOC dashboard instead of a vanity-metric wall, calculate MTTD and MTTR from real timestamps, translate technical SOC statistics into a leadership-ready risk report, and design a SOAR playbook (trigger, steps, IF/THEN branches) for a repeatable scenario while correctly identifying what still requires human judgment — the complete, vendor-neutral SOC operating model this path's next course specializes into Microsoft Sentinel, Defender XDR, and KQL.
